title: Three Units of Digit Weight
statement: How many positive integers less than $10^{25}$ have decimal digits that sum to $3$ and are divisible by $37$?
hints: A number whose digits sum to $3$ can be built by adding three powers of $10$, possibly with repeats. Write it this way and consider which exponents are allowed.
Work modulo $37$. Since $999 = 27 \cdot 37$, we have $10^3 \equiv 1 \pmod{37}$, so the residue of a power of $10$ depends only on its exponent modulo $3$.

The powers of $10$ have residues $1$, $10$ and $26$ modulo $37$. Writing the number as a sum of three powers of $10$, test all the ways of adding three of these residues. The only sum that is a multiple of $37$ is $1 + 10 + 26$, so the three exponents must lie in different classes modulo $3$. Now count the exponents from $0$ to $24$ in each class and combine these counts.
solution:
Such an integer is $n=10^a+10^b+10^c$ with $0\le a\le b\le c\le 24$, and distinct multisets $\{a,b,c\}$ give distinct integers, since the digit in position $k$ is the multiplicity of $k$.

Since $999=27\cdot 37$, we have $10^3\equiv1 \pmod{37}$, so $10^k\equiv 1,10,26$ for $k\equiv0,1,2\pmod 3$ respectively (as $100\equiv 26$).

Sums of three residues from $\{1,10,26\}$, with repetition allowed, are
$$3,\ 12,\ 28,\ 21,\ 37,\ 53,\ 30,\ 46,\ 62,\ 78.$$
Only $37=1+10+26$ is divisible by $37$. So $37\mid n$ exactly when $a,b,c$ lie in three different classes modulo $3$.

In $\{0,\dots,24\}$ the classes $0,1,2 \pmod 3$ contain $9,8,8$ elements respectively. Choosing one exponent from each class gives $9\cdot8\cdot8=576$ integers.
